items.title: Wall Street Sees Inflation Easing Even With Oil Above $90

events.article_text:
Oil Prices Climb Above $106 as Iran Threatens More Tanker Attacks

Alex Kimani is a veteran finance writer, investor, engineer and researcher for Safehaven.com.

The U.S. Consumer Price Index (CPI) report is due to be released on Wednesday, with economists predicting that key inflation metrics continued to moderate in September despite elevated oil prices, giving the Fed room to slow down on interest rate hikes. For September, economists expect headline inflation growth to clock in at 0.5% month-over-month and 3.6%- 3.7% year-over-year, up from 0.4% m-o-m and 3.4% Y/Y in August. Meanwhile, core CPI, which excludes volatile energy and food prices, is seen climbing 0.2% in September, down from August’s 0.3%, with the annual core inflation rate expected to hold steady at 2.4%. Additionally, the probability of a Federal Reserve interest rate hike at the upcoming October 27–28 meeting has dropped to around 19% to 20%, down significantly from over 70% in late September.

“You’ve seen supply shocks create a sticky situation,” Jeffrey Schulze, head investment strategist at the Franklin Templeton Institute, told Morningstar, referring to oil supply disruptions, tariff shocks and AI-related consumer goods’ price spikes. “But as we move toward 2027, some of these risks are going to start to moderate. That moderation may already be underway. I think you see softening across the board [in September].”

While the headline inflation is already exposing the impact of rising crude prices, economists note that broader core inflation categories have remained insulated, showing little to no evidence of pass-through pricing. Airfares have absorbed the brunt of ongoing energy shocks, with price increases exceeding 2% m-o-m in both July and August and 25% Y/Y thanks to elevated jet fuel costs. Fuel represents roughly 17% to 21% of an airline's total operating expenses, making ticket pricing uniquely sensitive to oil price spikes. In contrast, pass-through effects for most retail and manufacturing sectors can take several months or even quarters to manifest. “I think that’s going to be something that potentially shows up closer toward the end of the year, rather than in the September release,” says Schulze.

Related: OPEC Sees Oil Demand Growth Surging to 2.6 Million Bpd in 2027

U.S. oil and fuel prices have come down from recent highs but remain elevated. Brent crude for December delivery fell 2.0% to trade at $104.60 per barrel at 7.00 am ET on Tuesday, while WTI crude for November delivery declined by a similar margin to change hands at $91.89/bbl. Meanwhile, the average price of gasoline across the U.S. clocked in at $4.3413 per gallon on Tuesday, down from $4.8133/gal a month ago but much higher than around $2.98/gal before the war broke out in late February. Unfortunately, diesel prices have hardly budged, currently averaging $6.2787/gal from $6.3151 a week ago.

Last week, U.S. President Donald Trump struck a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to supply Russian diesel to U.S. and global markets in an effort to curb soaring fuel prices. Russia has pledged to release more than 300,000 metric tons (approx. 2.25 million barrels) of diesel fuel immediately, with an additional 500,000 metric tons scheduled for delivery in November 2026. Russia will then release 1 million metric tons following the November allocation, with a potential 3 million metric tons also in the cards depending on the condition of Russian oil refineries.

As part of the deal, the U.S. Treasury Department issued a general license suspending sanctions on Russian diesel exports until April 7, 2027, although other assets such as those held in American banks remain frozen. Hardly surprisingly, the agreement has sparked bipartisan opposition in Congress, with a group of both Republican and Democratic senators pointing out that the move violates a 2022 law banning Russian energy imports. European leaders have also criticized the temporary carve-out, arguing that pressure on Moscow ought to be increased rather than eased.

However, the deal’s biggest critics have been energy experts, who have aptly noted that the deliveries are likely to have minimal impact on fuel prices. To wit, the initial delivery of ~2.25 million barrels is hardly enough to meet the United States’ consumption for a single day, estimated at ~4.1 million barrels. Those volumes look even more puny in a global middle distillates market which remains badly squeezed. Ukrainian drone and missile strikes have decimated Russia's energy infrastructure, slashing Russian diesel production by nearly 30% and forcing Moscow to restrict or ban some of its own fuel exports earlier in the year in a bid to protect domestic supplies. Prior to the attacks, Russian diesel exports averaged more than 3 million metric tons per month (~1,000,000 barrels per day).

analysis.tldr: Cooling inflation in the U.S. makes the American central bank less likely to raise interest rates, which keeps global financial markets steady and helps protect the Indian rupee from heavy selling pressure.
the_story: The U.S. Consumer Price Index (CPI, a measure of price changes) report is due Wednesday, with economists expecting inflation to moderate in September despite elevated oil prices.
The probability of a U.S. Federal Reserve interest rate hike at the October 27–28 meeting has dropped to around 19% to 20%, down from over 70% in late September.

U.S. President Donald Trump struck a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to supply Russian diesel to lower fuel prices, temporarily lifting sanctions on Russian diesel exports until April 7, 2027.
Brent crude for December delivery fell 2.0% to trade at $104.60 per barrel, while WTI crude fell to $91.89/bbl, though prices remain elevated compared to historical levels.
analysis.what_happened: Even though oil prices remain high, economic reports suggest overall U.S. inflation is cooling down. Because price pressures are easing, the U.S. central bank faces much lower pressure to aggressively raise interest rates, calming global investors who feared tighter monetary policies.
analysis.analogy: It is like a family that was worried about rising grocery bills suddenly seeing prices steady, meaning they no longer have to panic-cut their other spending or borrow money at higher costs.
why_it_matters_india: When U.S. inflation cools, the U.S. Federal Reserve (America's central bank) is less likely to raise interest rates.
Lower or stable U.S. interest rates mean international investors don't pull all their money out of developing countries like India to chase safe U.S. returns.
This stable flow of foreign money prevents heavy outflows from Indian markets.
As a result, the rupee avoids sharp downward pressure, keeping imported items like crude oil from becoming unpredictably more expensive for India.

impacts.rationale: Fewer U.S. interest rate hikes keep global capital from rushing back to America, supporting the rupee and making imports slightly cheaper for Indians.
Global crude oil prices softening slightly helps keep domestic fuel and transport cost pressures in check, which is good for household budgets.
Lower chances of aggressive U.S. interest rate hikes improve global market sentiment, encouraging foreign investors to keep money in Indian equities.

watch_next: The official U.S. Consumer Price Index (CPI) inflation release
Further updates on the U.S.-Russia diesel supply agreement and political pushback in Congress
analysis.caveats: Geopolitical shocks or unexpected spikes in global crude oil could quickly reverse inflation expectations.

analysis.tldr: When the Reserve Bank of India spends its savings to protect our currency, it means importing goods like crude oil becomes more expensive for everyone.
the_story: India's foreign exchange reserves (money stored by the central bank in foreign currencies and gold) have fallen for the fourth week in a row to $734.6 billion.
This is down from a recent peak of $785.71 billion reached on September 4.
The Reserve Bank of India [RBI, India's central bank that controls money supply and interest rates] stepped into the market to support the rupee [India's currency] as it faced downward pressure.

The rupee's drop is being driven by high oil prices, rising US Treasury yields [interest rates paid by the US government to borrow money], and foreign equity outflows [money pulled out of Indian stocks by overseas investors].
analysis.what_happened: India's stored foreign money pot shrank because the Reserve Bank of India used those funds to buy rupees and stop the currency from falling too fast. This pressure on the rupee happened because global oil prices are high, international investors are pulling money out of India, and US government borrowing rates are rising.
analysis.analogy: It is like a shopkeeper dipping into their emergency cash savings day after day to pay for rising store costs because local customers are paying with less valuable money.
why_it_matters_india: Global factors like high US bond yields and expensive oil pull foreign money out of India -> This pushes the rupee down.
To stop the rupee from crashing too fast, the RBI sells its foreign cash reserves -> Total reserves drop to $734.6 billion.
A weaker rupee makes imported items like crude oil costlier -> This can push up everyday inflation (the rate at which prices rise) in India.
A shrinking reserve pot also leaves the country with a smaller financial safety cushion if global shocks worsen.

impacts.rationale: Continuous outflows and high oil prices put downward pressure on the currency, making imports pricier for everyday people.
The central bank keeps spending its dollar stash to defend the rupee, reducing our national financial safety buffer.
A weaker rupee and high oil prices mean fuel and imported goods cost more, which is bad for household budgets.

watch_next: Whether US Treasury yields continue to rise or cool down
The total size of India's foreign exchange reserves in next week's RBI data
analysis.caveats: If global oil prices suddenly drop or foreign investors start pouring money back into Indian stocks, the pressure on the rupee could ease quickly.

events.headline: A changing climate is reshaping India’s infectious disease risks

items.title: A changing climate is reshaping India’s infectious disease risks
items.summary: When extreme weather events occur, the damage is usually measured in collapsed buildings, damaged roads and flooded homes. But the aftermath also brings a less visible threat. Heatwaves, droughts, erratic rainfall and flash floods, in combination or alone, also reshape the ecology of diseases. They can affect how long pathogens survive, change the distribution of […]

events.article_text:
If you liked this story, share it with other people.

When extreme weather events occur, the damage is usually measured in collapsed buildings, damaged roads and flooded homes. But the aftermath also brings a less visible threat.

Heatwaves, droughts, erratic rainfall and flash floods, in combination or alone, also reshape the ecology of diseases. They can affect how long pathogens survive, change the distribution of disease-carrying insects and bring people, animals and pathogens into closer contact, increasing the risk of outbreaks in new places at unexpected times.

The latest assessment report by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change has warned that heatwaves and extreme rainfall events are projected to increase in the coming years. A 2025 study by IPE Global, an international development consultancy, and Esri India, a GIS mapping company, warns that extreme weather could become more severe by 2030, with heatwaves projected to double in major cities and extreme rainfall events expected to rise by 43% across the country.

Health experts state that we need to factor in and prevent climate-related outbreaks rather than simply responding to them.

The World Meteorological Organisation (WMO) reports that the past decade has witnessed some of the worst floods on record. India, too, has experienced devastating floods, including those in Mumbai in 2025 and Kerala in 2018.

“Heavy rainfall and flooding create ideal conditions for the emergence and spread of infections,” shares Surya Prasad, a consultant physician at Manipal Hospital, Bengaluru. “Floodwater overwhelms sewage systems and mixes human and animal waste into water sources, while warmer temperatures help pathogens survive longer.”

Some bacterial diarrhoeal diseases often peak during warmer, wetter conditions. A 21-year study from Kolkata, covering data from 1999 to 2019, found a biannual pattern in cholera cases, with peaks coinciding with rising summer temperatures and the onset of the monsoon.

Hepatitis A and E often see a rise in cases during the monsoon and post-monsoon months. In Delhi and Mumbai, major hepatitis E outbreaks have been linked to sewage entering water supplies after heavy monsoon rains.

A study conducted in Chennai found that the risk of hospitalisation for gastrointestinal illnesses was 60% higher in the 15 days following an extreme rainfall event.

But recent studies have also found that climate change is making these seasonal patterns unpredictable; it can change when and where infections appear. “Earlier, the cases of Hepatitis A, Hepatitis E and cholera were largely seen during the high temperatures of the pre-monsoon season. But over the past 10 years, we have been seeing these infections more frequently, and throughout the year,” Prasad elaborated.

Floods can also change the way pathogens move between animals and people. Flash floods can drive rodents out of sewers, burrows and other hiding places, while contaminated water can carry pathogens into homes and other areas, Prasad explained.

Leptospirosis, a zoonotic disease, shows a strong seasonal pattern, with more than 85% of annual cases occurring during and immediately after the monsoon. The bacteria that cause the disease spread through the urine of infected animals and can survive in contaminated water or soil for weeks to months.

“Rats are the primary hosts of Leptospira. During the monsoon, flooding drives them out of sewers, burrows and other hiding places into homes and drains. Their urine can contaminate water, food and surfaces, increasing the risk of infection, particularly during floods in cities,” said Prasad.

According to Integrated Disease Surveillance Project data, after the 2018 flood, Kerala witnessed 1,318 leptospirosis cases, including 53 deaths.

“Extreme weather events, such as intense rain or those leading to a natural disaster, can change the risk of specific infectious diseases,” explained Gautam Menon, a professor of Physics and Biology at Ashoka University, and the former director of the university’s Centre for Climate Change and Sustainability.

The effects are not limited to waterborne infections. Changes in temperature and rainfall can alter the breeding, behaviour and distribution of mosquitoes and other disease vectors, Menon explained. Warmer conditions can allow mosquitoes to survive and breed for longer, potentially expanding the geographic and seasonal window for diseases such as dengue, malaria and Zika.

In the Himalayan foothills, rising temperatures and shifting rainfall patterns are allowing malaria-carrying Anopheles mosquitoes to persist in areas and at elevations previously considered too cold for them. In 2024, Pune reported surges in Zika virus infections following heavy monsoon rains and flooding.

It is not only excessive water that poses a health risk. Droughts and prolonged water shortages can intensify the risk of infection in different ways.

A 2023 study found that as water sources shrink, people, livestock and wildlife may increasingly congregate around the same limited sources, increasing the chances of pathogen transmission. Other studies have linked overcrowding with the increase of pathogen transmission. Communities may also be forced to rely on unsafe or alternative sources of water, including those shared with domestic animals, increasing opportunities for contact and zoonotic disease transmission.

Less water for washing, food preparation and sanitation creates further opportunities for infection. Water collected from tankers or communal taps stored in large containers for long periods creates new sites for disease vectors such as mosquitoes to breed.

Extreme weather does not create disease risks in isolation. In India, the consequences are often amplified by weaknesses in basic infrastructure.

analysis.tldr: Rising extreme weather makes disease outbreaks more unpredictable and frequent, which could increase household medical expenses and strain public healthcare systems.
the_story: Climate change impacts the ecology of diseases by altering pathogen survival, changing insect distribution, and bringing humans, animals, and pathogens closer together.
A 2025 study by IPE Global and Esri India warns that heatwaves in major cities are projected to double and extreme rainfall events are expected to rise by 43% by 2030.
Heavy rainfall and floods overwhelm sewage systems, mixing waste into water supplies and causing surges in waterborne infections like cholera, Hepatitis A and E, and leptospirosis.
Rising temperatures and changing rainfall patterns allow mosquitoes to breed for longer periods and spread to new areas, leading to surges in dengue, malaria, and Zika.
Droughts and water shortages also increase risks by forcing people and animals to share limited water sources and reducing water available for washing and sanitation.
analysis.what_happened: Extreme weather events like heatwaves, droughts, erratic rainfall, and flash floods are reshaping infectious disease risks in India. According to experts cited in the article, these weather shifts help germs survive longer, push disease-carrying rodents out of flooded sewers, and expand the geographic zones where mosquitoes can breed.
analysis.analogy: It is like a messy kitchen where a leaking roof ruins your food storage and brings in pests all at once, forcing you to spend extra time and money fixing problems you did not budget for.
why_it_matters_india: Extreme weather events cause urban flooding and water contamination.
Contaminated water and displaced rodents lead to spikes in waterborne and animal-borne diseases like cholera and leptospirosis.
Families face higher out-of-pocket medical expenses and lost workdays due to sudden illness.
Public health infrastructure and insurance companies experience heavier claims and operational pressures.

impacts.target: Healthcare and hospital stocks (e.g., Apollo Hospitals, Max Healthcare)
impacts.rationale: Higher patient admissions for infectious diseases can increase hospital revenues, though it reflects a negative social trend.

impacts.target: Indian pharmaceutical stocks focusing on anti-infectives (e.g., Cipla, Sun Pharma)
impacts.rationale: Increased incidence of waterborne and vector-borne diseases drives up demand for specific medicines and treatments.

impacts.target: Health insurance sector claims payout ratio
impacts.rationale: More hospitalizations due to climate-linked outbreaks mean insurers pay out more claims, which can eventually lead to higher premium costs for ordinary citizens.

watch_next: Updates on urban flood management and sewage infrastructure projects in major cities like Mumbai, Delhi, and Chennai
Government disease surveillance reports following heavy monsoon or flood events
analysis.caveats: The article outlines long-term climate projections and historical disease patterns, but the exact timing and severity of future disease outbreaks remain unpredictable.

events.headline: Conflict in the Red Sea is forcing cloud giants to find a new route for the internet

items.title: Conflict in the Red Sea is forcing cloud giants to find a new route for the internet
items.summary: Fishermen motor past a commercial vessel anchored off Yemen's coast at Bab al-Mandeb, in the straits connecting the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean on September 12, 2026. Yemen's Houthis took over on September 11, 2026, a Red Sea island of Mayyun that is located in the middle of the Bab al-Mandeb shipping lane, completing their push to control the area, a local government official and eyewitnesses told AFP. Hundreds of people have died since the Iran-backed Houthis launched an offensive around Bab al-Mandab, a vital artery for Saudi oil exports. (Photo by AFP via Getty Image

events.article_text:
U.S. cloud giants are facing steep prices to secure backup internet routes around the Red Sea as fighting rages over the Red Sea strait that carries most data cables between Europe and Asia.

More than 90% of data capacity between Europe and Asia runs through cables under the Red Sea. The cables enter the sea at Bab al-Mandab, a strait less than 32 kilometers (20 miles) wide between Yemen and the African nations of Djibouti and Eritrea.

The Houthis, a U.S.-designated terrorist organization, seized Yemen’s side of the strait in September, including the island of Mayyun. On October 5, Saudi-backed government forces said they had retaken key positions around the strait and the port of Mocha — claims the Houthis denied.

In September, Google bought a pair of fiber strands running along Turkish state pipelines, paying two to three times the roughly 6 million euros ($7 million) that newer lines crossing Turkey are expected to cost, said a person familiar with the deal, requesting anonymity because the details are not public. Long-distance fiber is usually sold with a single upfront payment covering 15 years or more of use. Buyers also pay a separate annual fee for maintenance.

Microsoft said on September 23 that it plans to invest more than $400 million in subsea and land links across the Middle East by 2030. Iraq also signed a contract with Qatari telecom company Ooredoo on September 10 to carry data toward Europe through an underground route from the southern port of Al-Faw.

Almost all major cloud companies are looking for backup routes around the Red Sea, the person told Rest of World. Google and Meta have started sending some live traffic through a land route across Iraq that they had previously held in reserve, the person said.

Google and Meta did not respond to Rest of World’s requests for comment by the time of publication.

With Yemen’s side of the strait now contested, a single cable cut there could take months to fix, because repair crews need permission and safety guarantees to work in the water, industry experts told Rest of World. Switching to another sea cable does not help because almost all of them pass through the same narrow gap, they said.

“You can have capacity on multiple cables, but if they’re all routed through the same tight expanse of water, suddenly your route resilience isn’t looking so resilient,” said Paul Brodsky, senior research manager at TeleGeography, a U.S. research firm that tracks telecommunications infrastructure worldwide. “The repair ship issue is very real.”

Three Red Sea cables were damaged in 2024, most likely by the anchor of a drifting cargo ship that a missile launched by the Iran-backed Houthis had disabled. Those repairs took months because crews had to wait a long time for permits, Brodsky said.

“Depending on the availability of a repair ship, a cable repair might take one to two weeks,” Doug Madory, head of internet analysis at Santa Clara-based Infoblox, which runs core network services and tracks how internet traffic moves, told Rest of World. “But the last time there were cable cuts in this body of water, repairs took months because the repair ships needed assurances they would not be fired upon.”

Google, Meta, Microsoft, and Amazon use about three-quarters of the world’s international internet bandwidth, according to TeleGeography. When Iranian drones struck Amazon’s data centers in the United Arab Emirates and Bahrain in March, bank and payment apps in the region stopped working, and U.S. software company Snowflake reported service disruptions.

Since the start of September, cloud companies have been telling operators the minimum number of fiber strands they will start using, and by when, Martin Frank, a strategic adviser at IQ Networks, an Iraqi company that sells capacity on a fiber line it built from southern Iraq to the Turkish border, told Rest of World.

Cloud companies will likely test their land backups so they are ready if a sea cable breaks, Madory said. Until then, most of their data will keep flowing under the sea.

“Submarine cable routes are much cheaper, which is why they are so preferred,” he said. “I would expect land route alternatives to remain dormant until pressed into service due to a cable cut.”

Cloud companies have been hoping Yemen would settle down under a normal administration, Frank said. What would end that hope is what he called an Afghanistan scenario, in which the international community accepts the reality on the ground as the new normal.

“From what I see and hear, I would say that this scenario is getting more and more priced in by the day,” Frank said.

African companies race to adopt American and Chinese AI, with little attention paid to safety.

AI data centers are driving demand for memory chips, pushing phone makers to raise prices and abandon some of their most affordable models.

From batteries and solar panels to drones and satellites, China is building tech capabilities that extend well beyond AI, writes Steve Feldstein in his new book, "Bytes and Bullets: Global Rivalries, Big Tech, and the New Shape of Modern Warfare."

analysis.tldr: Fighting in the Red Sea is forcing global tech giants to pay high prices for backup internet routes, which could eventually make digital services and cloud infrastructure costlier for businesses everywhere.
the_story: More than 90% of data capacity between Europe and Asia runs through cables under the Red Sea, passing through the Bab al-Mandab strait.
In September, the Houthis seized Yemen's side of the strait, though Saudi-backed government forces claimed to retake key positions around October 5.

Major tech companies like Google, Meta, and Microsoft are paying steep prices for backup land routes through places like Turkey and Iraq because underwater cables face high risks of being damaged and taking months to fix.
analysis.what_happened: Fighting around the Red Sea strait has put vital internet cables at risk of damage, with repair ships struggling to get safety guarantees. Because of this danger, US cloud giants are rushing to secure expensive land-based backup routes for internet traffic instead of relying solely on cheap underwater cables.
analysis.analogy: It is like having all your goods delivered through a single narrow mountain road that is suddenly blocked by fighting, forcing you to pay twice as much to truck your goods through a much longer detour.
why_it_matters_india: Tech giants face higher operational costs to secure redundant internet routes around the troubled Red Sea region.
These rising infrastructure and data-transport expenses are absorbed by global tech providers.
Higher underlying digital costs can eventually translate into more expensive cloud and software services for Indian businesses and startups that rely on these global tech platforms.
This adds another layer of cost inflation to the digital economy alongside hardware and chip shortages.

impacts.target: IT services and software usage costs for businesses
impacts.rationale: As tech giants spend heavily on alternative land data routes, those costs may trickle down to corporate customers, which is bad for Indian tech-dependent firms.

impacts.target: Global cloud infrastructure spending by big tech
impacts.rationale: Companies like Google, Microsoft, and Meta are actively investing hundreds of millions in land and subsea alternatives, driving up overall capital expenditures.

watch_next: Further updates on security and repair ship access in the Red Sea strait
Announcements from major cloud providers regarding price adjustments for data transmission
analysis.caveats: The article focuses primarily on Western tech giants and Middle Eastern land routes, so the exact impact on individual Indian consumer internet bills remains indirect.

events.headline: Rupee stopgap: RBI's new props have boosted its external value but this only spells momentary relief

items.title: Rupee stopgap: RBI's new props have boosted its external value but this only spells momentary relief
items.summary: The central bank’s emergency measures to support India’s currency hint of panic. They could also make risk-hedging dearer. For real relief from exchange rate weakness, the country's macro dynamics will need to move in the rupee’s favour.

events.article_text:
The Reserve Bank of India’s (RBI) emergency measures to support the rupee have boosted its value, but are unlikely to do very much beyond buying us time. On Saturday, barely three days after Governor Sanjay Malhotra declared that he thought the currency was undervalued, the central bank announced a set of new props.

True, the rupee might have been trading below its ‘real effective exchange rate’ (REER), but markets go by supply and demand as well as sentiment, not artificial constructs like the REER, which tracks a trade-weighted basket of currencies. And the harsh fact is that today’s forces of demand and supply do not favour our currency.

On the contrary. For too long have successive governors said RBI does not target any level for the rupee but only manages its market volatility. Few believe that.

Yet, its latest move came as a surprise. More so since RBI had not just wrapped up one of its largest ever exercises to shore up its forex reserves, it raised its policy rate last week. On Monday, the rupee rallied almost 1% against the dollar. On Tuesday, it gained another 0.4%.

Key among the measures is a special dollar window for state-run oil companies to buy dollars. This means that Indian Oil Corp, Hindustan Petroleum and Bharat Petroleum will no longer buy forex in the spot market for their imports, and to that extent, pressure on the rupee will ease.

The three oil companies are estimated to require about $300 million daily to pay their crude import bills. Their heavy and recurring demand for dollars adds to buying pressure in the spot market, which weakens the rupee if it is not balanced with dollar supply. By selling oil importers dollars directly, RBI aims to moderate that weakening force and help the rupee attain stability.

How long the effects last, of course, would depend on larger factors. The last time RBI hit such an emergency button was in 2013 during the ‘taper tantrum,’ when its clutch of actions slowed the rupee’s slide temporarily.

The key word here is ‘temporarily.’ The reality is that the domestic currency will not be relieved of pressure so long as global oil prices rule high (India imports almost 90% of its needs), global bond yields harden, capital inflows sputter and the dollar index stays high.

Another significant factor in all this is the government’s effort to shield fuel users from this year’s oil shock. If retail prices are allowed to rise, a reduction in discretionary demand may help reduce energy imports. But that’s a call for central policymakers to take.

The forex window is only one of the measures taken by RBI to bolster the rupee, which has dropped by almost 6% in 2026 so far. Among other steps, the most important is a drastic reduction—to $5 million from $100 million—of RBI’s cap on the size of derivative transactions that can be done without proof of underlying exchange risk exposure.

Plus, RBI barred authorized dealers from letting traders rebook cancelled rupee-linked forex derivative contracts, thereby making currency management vastly more expensive and rigid for businesses.

Grumbles have arisen over a 20% forex reserve requirement placed on some derivative trades; this acts as a tax on risk mitigation in its effect and is likely to drive up hedging costs that banks will likely pass on to clients.

These moves may give the rupee breathing space today, as they already seem to have, but do not address the currency’s underlying stress points. For a reliably stable exchange rate, macro dynamics must shift in the rupee’s favour.

analysis.tldr: The RBI's emergency steps have given the rupee a temporary boost, but everyday costs like petrol will stay under pressure unless global oil prices and economic conditions truly settle.
the_story: Governor Sanjay Malhotra declared the rupee undervalued, followed shortly by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) introducing a surprise set of new emergency props on Saturday.

The RBI created a special dollar window for state-run oil companies (Indian Oil Corp, Hindustan Petroleum, Bharat Petroleum) to buy dollars directly, removing their daily $300 million demand from the open spot market.
The rupee rallied almost 1% against the dollar on Monday and gained another 0.4% on Tuesday following the announcement.

The RBI also drastically cut the cap on certain derivative transactions without proof of risk from $100 million to $5 million, and barred traders from rebooking cancelled rupee-linked forex derivative contracts.

The article notes the rupee has dropped by almost 6% in 2026 so far, and these measures only buy time rather than fixing underlying pressures like high global oil prices and strong global bond yields.
analysis.what_happened: The RBI stepped in with emergency market controls to defend the sliding rupee. Because state oil companies need about $300 million daily to buy crude oil, their constant demand for dollars weakens the rupee. By supplying those dollars directly and making currency derivative trades much more restrictive and costly, the RBI successfully reduced immediate selling pressure on the rupee.
analysis.analogy: It is like a grocery shop owner putting a heavy wooden beam against a shaking door to stop it from blowing open in a storm; it holds the door shut for now, but it does not stop the storm outside.
why_it_matters_india: RBI sets up a direct dollar window for state-run oil companies -> oil firms stop buying dollars in the open market.
Open market demand for foreign currency drops -> immediate downward pressure on the rupee eases, causing it to rally briefly.
Simultaneously, RBI slashes derivative transaction caps and imposes strict rules -> hedging costs for businesses go up.
Global oil prices remain high and capital inflows sputter -> fundamental pressures persist, meaning the rupee's relief will likely be temporary.

impacts.rationale: The RBI's direct dollar support and restrictions on traders have given the currency a short-term lift, which is good for lowering import costs temporarily.
While the rupee gained slightly, India still imports nearly 90% of its oil and global prices remain high, meaning retail relief depends entirely on broader government policy choices.

watch_next: Global crude oil prices and whether they remain high
Whether the government decides to adjust retail fuel prices or let them rise
analysis.caveats: If global oil prices spike further or global bond yields harden, these emergency props may fail to keep the rupee stable for long.

events.headline: Madagascar launches safeguard investigation on certain confectionary

items.title: Madagascar launches safeguard investigation on certain confectionary
items.summary: On 12 October 2026, Madagascar notified the WTO’s Committee on Safeguards that it had initiated on 9 October 2026 a safeguard investigation on imports of sugar confectionary as well as chocolate and cocoa confectionary.

events.article_text:
In the notification Madagascar indicated, among other things, as follows (provisional English translation):

"4. Provide a point of contact for the investigation and identify the preferred means for corresponding.

The point of contact would be available to respond to enquiries relating to the procedures applicable to the investigation.

Boulevard de Tokyo, Ankadievo Alasora, Antananarivo 103 - Madagascar

5. Provide the deadlines and procedures for importers, exporters and other interested parties to present evidence and their views, including: (i) deadlines and procedures for Members and exporters to identify themselves as interested parties, if so required, to participate in the investigation and (ii) the date of an intended public hearing as provided for in Article 3.1. [..]

Interested parties have 30 days from the initiation of the investigation to make themselves known to the ANMCC, submit their comments, and request a questionnaire. Responses to the questionnaire and other relevant information must be submitted within 30 working days. Public hearings may be held at the request of the parties or on the ANMCC's own initiative. If responses are not submitted within the prescribed deadlines, or if the information provided is inaccurate or incomplete, determinations may be made on the basis of the best information available."

The notification is available in G/SG/N/6/MDG/21. (Currently available in French only)

A safeguard investigation seeks to determine whether increased imports of a product are causing, or are threatening to cause, serious injury to a domestic industry.

During a safeguard investigation, importers, exporters and other interested parties may present evidence and views and respond to the presentations of other parties.

A WTO member may take a safeguard action (i.e. restrict imports of a product temporarily) only if the increased imports of the product are found to be causing, or threatening to cause, serious injury.

Problems viewing this page? If so, please contact [email protected] giving details of the operating system and web browser you are using.

analysis.tldr: A tiny procedural trade investigation in Madagascar will have virtually zero impact on your daily life, the Indian rupee, or your savings in India.
the_story: Madagascar has officially launched a safeguard investigation into certain types of confectionery (sweets and candies).
The investigation is being handled by the ANMCC (the local authority named in the notice located in Antananarivo, Madagascar).
Interested parties such as importers and exporters have 30 days from the start of the investigation to make themselves known, submit comments, and request a questionnaire.
A safeguard investigation is a tool where a country checks if a sudden surge in imports is hurting its local manufacturing businesses.
The notification provides contact details, a physical address on Boulevard de Tokyo in Antananarivo, and warns that incomplete responses will lead to decisions based on available information.
analysis.what_happened: Madagascar started a formal check to see if imported sweets are harming its local sweet-making businesses. This happens through a process set up by the World Trade Organization (an international body that handles global rules of trade between countries), allowing local authorities to look into import data and hear from affected businesses.
analysis.analogy: It is like a local grocery shop owner asking customers to pause and check if buying too many cheap imported chocolates from outside is putting the neighborhood bakery out of business.
why_it_matters_india: Madagascar launches a safeguard investigation into specific imported sweets.
Traders and companies around the world have 30 days to submit evidence and questionnaires to Madagascar's ANMCC office.
The investigation looks at whether these imports cause serious injury to local businesses in Madagascar.
Because this is hyper-specific to Madagascar and confectioneries, it has no meaningful connection to major Indian macroeconomic factors like inflation, oil prices, or currency rates.

impacts.rationale: No direct link exists between a trade notice in Madagascar and India's currency, so any movement would be driven by completely unrelated global economic factors.
Large Indian stock prices do not react to minor local confectionery investigations in East Africa.

watch_next: Future updates from the ANMCC in Madagascar on whether they decide to restrict confectionery imports.
analysis.caveats: Only the headline and standard WTO procedural text were available, confirming it is an isolated regulatory filing with no broader economic spillover.

events.headline: How Taiwan Activates Beijing’s Chosen Fear

items.title: How Taiwan Activates Beijing’s Chosen Fear
items.summary: The standard explanations for why Taiwan is so important to the Chinese Communist Party are familiar: territorial integrity, credibility of deterrence commitments, great power competition with the United States, the strategic value of the first island chain, and the semiconductor industry concentrated in TSMC’s fabrication facilities. These explanations work, but they don’t tell the whole story. Rational strategic calculation does not produce a posture in which a nuclear-armed state with the world’s second-largest economy treats a democratic island of 23 million people as a permanent, non-nego

events.article_text:
The Chinese Communist Party’s posture toward Taiwan is driven not primarily by strategic calculation, at least not in the way it is understood from outside. Its posture is driven by a political trauma the party has consistently chosen to adopt and emphasize: three millennia of Chinese political history, interpreted through what I call the fragmentation pattern. This describes the situation in which a displaced regime establishes a rival power node that continues to claim sovereignty over the whole. It then either reconquers the center or is destroyed. The fact that this binary is false is irrelevant: It is the story that has been embraced, and cynically cultivated.

Beijing is finding that echoed civilizational trauma invoked in the name of regime stability is not easily discarded. The resulting ways in which the party is obliged to act are shaped by this narrative. For the United States, the consequence is significant: Deterrence built around imposing costs may fail if Beijing perceives inaction itself as a threat to regime survival. Understanding the historical template through which the Chinese Communist Party interprets Taiwan is therefore necessary to understanding what will deter Beijing and where U.S. strategy is most likely to miscalculate.

Victoria Tin-bor Hui’s comparative analysis of Chinese and European state formation argues that neither Chinese unification nor European fragmentation was structurally inevitable: Both were the products of strategic choices, particularly the self-strengthening reforms that allowed dominant states to absorb rivals. She argues specifically against geographic determinism in favor of political agency: The Chinese heartland was just as prone to political fragmentation as any other region. There was no foreordained pattern. China was never destined to be a centrally controlled single state. The fact that it happened repeatedly has no intrinsic value, but tremendous propaganda worth to anyone wishing to point to a tradition of political unity. The patterns of history may not themselves be deterministic, but they are politically useful, and the Chinese motif of unification has proved extraordinarily useful to the Chinese Communist Party.

Fragmentation and reunification have been the defining rhythm of Chinese political life, and a generation of Chinese citizens — including today’s cadres — have been schooled in it the way American officers are schooled in the lessons of Pearl Harbor and the Cuban Missile Crisis. On both counts the events themselves were real and documented, but American education focuses on the events as a product of their time and geopolitical circumstance, not a historical motif. Mark Edward Lewis’s histories of the early Chinese empires document the cycle from its origins: the Warring States period that preceded Qin unification in 221 B.C. and the collapse of the Han into the Three Kingdoms. The pattern repeated through the Sui, the Tang, the Song partition, and the Yuan Mongol conquest. The Ming expelled the Mongol Yuan, reunified China, then fell to the Manchu Qing. Southern Ming loyalist courts persisted for nearly two decades claiming continued legitimate authority over all of their former empire. The Qing collapse in 1912 produced warlordism, civil war, and left China vulnerable to Japanese invasion.

The lesson that the modern Chinese Communist Party has chosen to learn, and rely on, is this: When a Chinese dynasty falls, the displaced regime or its successors do not accept the loss and establish an independent state. They relocate, claim continued sovereignty over the whole, and persist as a standing challenge to the legitimacy of whoever holds the center. The Eastern Jin fled south after the fall of the Western Jin and ruled from Nanjing for over a century while non-Chinese dynasties held the north. The Southern Ming established rival courts after the Manchu conquest and fought on for nearly 20 years. The conclusion that can be drawn if only considering these cases is that the rival claimant represented an existential challenge to the legitimacy of the ruling dynasty, and the dynasty that tolerated the rival claimant’s existence was eventually judged to have failed the fundamental test of governance.

That test has a name that is so familiar it has become a cliché, which is precisely why its operational significance is underestimated: the Mandate of Heaven. The concept, which dates to the early Zhou dynasty, is not divine-right doctrine in the European sense. It is much better understood as a performance standard. Dingxin Zhao traces how the Western Han fused Confucian moral legitimation and Legalist administrative control, with the mandate as the test of that system: The ruler held it as long as he governed competently, maintained order, and preserved the unity of the realm. The mandate’s withdrawal is demonstrated by natural disasters, popular unrest, and above all by the fracture of political unity — when the ruler morally fails.

The existence of a rival claimant is, then, evidence that the mandate is in doubt and represents a direct refutation of the regime’s legitimacy. It is part of the evaluative framework through which political legitimacy has been assessed far beyond living memory, and it is the framework that Beijing has chosen to evaluate itself by. Zheng Wang’s research on Chinese political memory shows how the party maintains this framework through its schools. The patriotic education campaign launched after 1989 made the choice of which history to remember, putting the Century of Humiliation and the equation of national unity with national survival at the center of Chinese identity. Wang, borrowing the psychiatrist Vamik Volkan’s term, calls this a chosen trauma. The template is not merely inherited but actively reinforced by the state. This reinforcement only further constrains Beijing on the Taiwan question. To back down becomes a blow to legitimacy out of all proportion to its actual significance.

Taiwa

analysis.tldr: Tensions around Taiwan are driven by deep-rooted historical fears in Beijing, meaning any conflict could disrupt global technology supply chains and hit Indian electronics manufacturing.
the_story: The Chinese Communist Party's posture toward Taiwan is driven by a political trauma it has chosen to emphasize, known as the 'fragmentation pattern' where displaced regimes claim sovereignty.

Scholars like Victoria Tin-bor Hui and Mark Edward Lewis show that while Chinese history featured repeated cycles of fragmentation and reunification from early empires to the Qing collapse, the narrative of inevitable unity is a political choice.
The modern Chinese Communist Party relies on the 'Mandate of Heaven' performance standard, where political unity is the ultimate test of competent governance.
Beijing's patriotic education campaign, launched after 1989, treats national unity as tied to national survival, making backing down on Taiwan an existential threat to regime legitimacy.
analysis.what_happened: An analysis of Beijing's political mindset argues that China's stance on Taiwan is not just about standard strategic planning. Instead, it is shaped by centuries-old historical narratives about political fragmentation and the 'Mandate of Heaven' [the ancient belief that a ruler's right to govern depends on maintaining complete unity and order]. Because Beijing treats a rival power like Taiwan as an existential threat to its own legitimacy, it leaves very little room to back down.
analysis.analogy: It is like a family business where an old feud is treated as a matter of life and death, so even a small family disagreement causes everyone to panic because they fear the whole household will collapse.
why_it_matters_india: Geopolitical tensions rise around Taiwan -> Global supply chains for advanced technology and semiconductors [microchips used in electronics] face major risks of disruption.
Semiconductor supply lines tighten -> Availability and prices of electronic components shift globally.
Global chip costs and availability fluctuate -> India's domestic electronics manufacturing and 'Make in India' expansion plans face operational hurdles and input cost pressures.
Global market uncertainty increases -> Foreign investors pull money out of emerging markets like India into safe havens, affecting local stock indices.

impacts.rationale: Global risk-off sentiment during geopolitical flare-ups usually causes foreign investors to pull money out of Indian equities, which hurts everyday investors.
Geopolitical fears drive investors worldwide toward safe havens like gold, making it costlier for Indian households to buy.
Broader economic instability and supply chain shocks can slow down global tech spending, which negatively impacts major Indian tech exporters.

watch_next: Statements from Beijing regarding military or political actions toward Taiwan
Global semiconductor export controls and tech supply chain announcements
analysis.caveats: The article text cuts off near the end, but the core thesis on historical framing and regime legitimacy is fully established.

history.title: A budget that broke the pension system in three days
history.what: A new British government announced large unfunded tax cuts. Within three days UK government bond yields spiked so violently that pension funds faced collapse, and the Bank of England had to step in with emergency bond buying. The Prime Minister resigned within seven weeks.
history.why: Pension funds had used a strategy called liability-driven investing, which borrows against bonds to match long-term obligations. It works while yields move gradually. When yields jumped, the funds faced collateral calls, and the only way to meet them was to sell the very bonds that were falling — pushing yields higher still. Hidden leverage almost nobody outside the industry had noticed.
history.impact: The pound hit an all-time low against the dollar. Mortgage rates jumped and hundreds of mortgage products were pulled within days. The government's entire fiscal plan was reversed.
history.policy: The Bank of England bought long-dated bonds for a strictly limited window to break the loop, then regulators forced pension funds to hold far larger liquidity buffers against exactly this scenario.
history.consequence: It established that a rich, stable country with its own currency can still be disciplined by the bond market within days. Finance ministers everywhere became noticeably more careful about announcing unfunded spending.
history.pattern: The dangerous leverage is the leverage nobody discusses, usually because it sits inside an institution everyone considers boring. Ask who is forced to sell when prices fall — forced sellers turn a move into a spiral.
history.india_echo: India's fiscal deficit and government borrowing programme are worth watching for this reason. A bond market's patience is not infinite, and when it runs out it runs out in days rather than quarters.
history.watch_for: Bond yields rising while the currency falls. Normally higher yields support a currency; when both move the wrong way together, the market is questioning the government's credibility rather than its interest rates.
